variants.candidate: Earth is what the fire leaves behind. Wood burns down to ash and ash is already soil, so every blaze ends as ground that something else can stand on. The flame spends itself and the field keeps the gift, dark and warm and ready for seed. What began as light becomes a place, and the place outlasts the fire that made it.
variants.original: Fire gives birth to earth, the old texts say: what burns comes down at last as ash, and ash settles into soil. Nothing bright is lost entirely. The flame that danced for an evening feeds the field for a generation, warmth pressed down into ground that will hold seeds long after the light is gone.

variants.candidate: Wood is what a fire is made of before it is a fire. The warmth sits in the grain of a dry branch for years, waiting on one spark, and once the branch takes the flame has its shape and its hours. Fed on green wood a fire smokes and sulks, and fed on seasoned wood it burns steady into the night and leaves embers hot enough to start the morning.
variants.original: Wood is warm by nature and fire sleeps inside it, the classics say, so every flame is fed by what was gathered before it: dry branches, stacked seasons, years of quiet growth surrendered to one bright hour. A fire is only ever as tall as its fuel. The blaze borrows everything from the forest.

variants.candidate: Water ends fire, the old texts say: the many overcome the few, and rain outlasts any blaze. Heat climbs and spreads wherever it finds fuel, and water is the one thing it cannot consume. Poured over a flame, water does not argue with it. It takes the heat into itself, rises as steam and leaves the ground cool and dark, and every fire that meets water learns its true size.
variants.original: The many prevail over the few, and so water commands fire: one flame meets the falling rain, and however bright it burned, the rain does not run out first. What survives learns to burn banked and careful. Rain is the blaze's schooling: after it, fire keeps its heat closer and wastes less light.

variants.candidate: Fire meets fire and neither has to fight the other for air, the old texts say: like lights shine on each other, and like seeks like. One flame set beside another takes nothing from it. Each feeds on what it was given and both grow brighter for the company, until the shared heat outruns what any single hearth can hold. Fire is the one element fed by its own kind and spent by it.
variants.original: Lights answer one another, the old histories say: flame set beside flame makes one blaze, brighter than the sum of what was lit. There is no reaction between them, only reinforcement, heat agreeing with heat. Such doubling warms whole houses, and it can also empty the woodpile twice as fast.

variants.candidate: Fire works metal, the old texts say: the forge softens the blade, and iron that held one shape for ages gives it up inside the heat. The flame does not break the ore, it loosens it until the hammer can ask for a new line. Every fire wants something hard to work on, and every finished blade keeps the warmth that once made it move.
variants.original: The refined prevails over the stubborn, and so fire works metal: in the furnace the hardest thing in the world goes soft, gives up its rock, and takes a finer form. Cold, metal refuses every argument. Heated, it flows like consent, and the smith reads the glow the way farmers read the sky.
